Five palcomagnetic sites were collected from the Bonny pluton, four sites from the Valhalla pluton, five sites from the feldspar porphyry dikes, three mafic dikes and three felsic, non-porphyritic dikes (Table 1). The Bonny pluton sites were collected over a 2 x 3 km area and constituted only 30% of the outcrop (the rest being the Vanda dike swarm). The Valhalla pluton sites were collected-3 km from Lake Vanda (Figure 3). Well-grouped and indistinguishable characteristic reinanent directions (south/southwest and shallow) were obtained at high unblocking temperatures (above 450øC) from the Bonny pluton and the Vanda dike sites (Table 1; Figures 2b and 2c). Measurements of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were made using a cryogenic magnetometer and/or a computerized fluxgate Molspin magnetometer (housed within Helmholtz coils) on one or more specimens. Pilot samples were progressively demagnetized using stepwise alternating field (AF) or thermal (TH) techniques to determine the best demagnetization procedure for each site. During AF demagnetization, steps of generally 5 to 10 mT up to a peak of 95 mT were used (minimum of eight steps), while during thermal demagnetization steps of generally 50øC or 100øC up to 500øC and then 10 ø or 20øC intervals up to a maximum of 600øC were used (minimum of 10 steps). Susceptibility measurements were made after each thermal demagnetization step to evaluate mineralogical changes associated with heating the specimen. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) experiments were carried out on representative specimens from the main sample locations. Magnetic saturation was obtained in fields of less than 300 mT and when combined with the observed unblocking temperature spectra suggest that the remanence is carried by titanomagnetite in the sampled intrusions. [Wilson, 1992]. Major tilting has not occurred in southern Victoria Land since the Devonian, because flat-lying Beacon strata rest unconformably on the granitoids. Tilting may have occurred prior to the Devonian but the consistency of the data over such a large region and within different intrusions of similar age sampled across known structural blocks argues against that. There does not appear to be any significant rotation associated with discrete fault blocks, as the trend of the lower Paleozoic lamprophyre and feldspar porphyry dikes are extremely consistent over a 100 x 300 km region [Janosy and Wilson, 1992]. The consistent normal polarity observed in the palcomagnetic data might suggest that either the igneous rocks were emplaced during a relatively short interval of time or that remagnetization has occurred. ins that developed along the margin of eastern North America in the early stages of formation of the Atlantic Ocean [Manspeizer, 1988]. Deposition in the basin is now known to span much of the the Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic [Cornet and Olsen, 1985] and was punctuated only by a brief igneous intrusive and extrusive episode just after the Triassic/Jurassic boundary [Olsen and Sues, 1986; Fowell et al., 1994] and dated at 201-202 Ma [Sutter, 1988; Dunning and Hodych, 1990]. The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. These climatic cycles constitute a basis for detailed lithostratigraphic correlation as well as chronological scaling. Early paleomagnetic work on Newark Supergroup rocks focused on the igneous units and found mostly normal polarity magnetizations [e.g., DuBois et al., 1957; Opdyke, 1961; Smith and Noltmier, 1979]. This contributed to the concept of a quiet or long normal polarity interval in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic [McElhinny and Burek, 1971; Perchesky and Khramov, 1973; Irving and Pullaiah, 1976; Haq et al., 1988]. Paleomagnetic study of about 2400 samples from nearly 7 km of core recovered at seven drill sites in the Newark continental rift basin of eastern North America provides a derailed history of geomagnetic reversals and paleolatitudinal motion for about 30 m.y. of the Late Triassic and earliest Jurassic (Carnian to Hettangian). The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. ins that developed along the margin of eastern North America in the early stages of formation of the Atlantic Ocean [Manspeizer, 1988]. Deposition in the basin is now known to span much of the the Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic [Cornet and Olsen, 1985] and was punctuated only by a brief igneous intrusive and extrusive episode just after the Triassic/Jurassic boundary [Olsen and Sues, 1986; Fowell et al., 1994] and dated at 201-202 Ma [Sutter, 1988; Dunning and Hodych, 1990]. The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. These climatic cycles constitute a basis for detailed lithostratigraphic correlation as well as chronological scaling. Early paleomagnetic work on Newark Supergroup rocks focused on the igneous units and found mostly normal polarity magnetizations [e.g., DuBois et al., 1957; Opdyke, 1961; Smith and Noltmier, 1979]. This contributed to the concept of a quiet or long normal polarity interval in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic [McElhinny and Burek, 1971; Perchesky and Khramov, 1973; Irving and Pullaiah, 1976; Haq et al., 1988]. ins that developed along the margin of eastern North America in the early stages of formation of the Atlantic Ocean [Manspeizer, 1988]. Deposition in the basin is now known to span much of the the Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic [Cornet and Olsen, 1985] and was punctuated only by a brief igneous intrusive and extrusive episode just after the Triassic/Jurassic boundary [Olsen and Sues, 1986; Fowell et al., 1994] and dated at 201-202 Ma [Sutter, 1988; Dunning and Hodych, 1990]. The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. These climatic cycles constitute a basis for detailed lithostratigraphic correlation as well as chronological scaling. Early paleomagnetic work on Newark Supergroup rocks focused on the igneous units and found mostly normal polarity magnetizations [e.g., DuBois et al., 1957; Opdyke, 1961; Smith and Noltmier, 1979]. This contributed to the concept of a quiet or long normal polarity interval in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic [McElhinny and Burek, 1971; Perchesky and Khramov, 1973; Irving and Pullaiah, 1976; Haq et al., 1988]. Division 1 is a relatively thin unit, generally massive at its base and becoming better bedded upward as the density of desiccation cracks and/or tubes (root or burrows) decreases. First removed with a maximum unblocking temperature of 300 ø to sometimes 400øC is a steep downward magnetization which we identify as a recent overprint and refer to as the A component. Magnetic susceptibility of samples from the Lockatong, Passaic, and Feltville Formations typically showed very large increases after heating to moderate to high temperatures, starting at about 550øC in the red and gray shales but by about 400øC in the darker gray to black shales (Figure 5). Paleomagnetic study of about 2400 samples from nearly 7 km of core recovered at seven drill sites in the Newark continental rift basin of eastern North America provides a derailed history of geomagnetic reversals and paleolatitudinal motion for about 30 m.y. of the Late Triassic and earliest Jurassic (Carnian to Hettangian). Northward drift of only about 7 ø is recorded in the continental sediments and minor interbedded basaltic lavas in the basin, from 2.5 ø to 6.5 ø north paleolatitude in the Carnian and from 6.5 ø to 9.5 ø north paleolatitude over the Norian-\"Rhaetian\" and the early Hettangian. A total of 59 polarity intervals, ranging from about 4 m to over 300 m in thickness, have been delineated in a composite stratigraphic section of 4660 m. Sampling and Laboratory Procedures A paleomagnetic sample plug was taken from what we judged to be the most favorable lithology within each core storage box (nominal 3 m interval). Most of the samples were from red sediments, but all lithologies including gray to black shales and the basalts were included as part of the regular sampling scheme. The sample plugs consisted of 2.5-cm- diameter cylinders drilled perpendicular to the core axis, inscribed in the upcore direction, and sliced into 2.2 cm long (~11 cm 3) specimens for paleomagnetic measurements. The specimens were stored, and demagnetization treatments and measurements of their natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were made within a low magnetic field environment (<300 !.tT) of a shielded room. ins that developed along the margin of eastern North America in the early stages of formation of the Atlantic Ocean [Manspeizer, 1988]. Deposition in the basin is now known to span much of the the Late Triassic to earliest Jurassic [Cornet and Olsen, 1985] and was punctuated only by a brief igneous intrusive and extrusive episode just after the Triassic/Jurassic boundary [Olsen and Sues, 1986; Fowell et al., 1994] and dated at 201-202 Ma [Sutter, 1988; Dunning and Hodych, 1990]. The lacustrine sediments that constitute much of the Newark Basin section record climatically induced lake level variations reflecting Milankovitch orbital forcing [Van Houten, 1964; Olsen, 1986]. These climatic cycles constitute a basis for detailed lithostratigraphic correlation as well as chronological scaling. Early paleomagnetic work on Newark Supergroup rocks focused on the igneous units and found mostly normal polarity magnetizations [e.g., DuBois et al., 1957; Opdyke, 1961; Smith and Noltmier, 1979]. This contributed to the concept of a quiet or long normal polarity interval in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic [McElhinny and Burek, 1971; Perchesky and Khramov, 1973; Irving and Pullaiah, 1976; Haq et al., 1988]. The NRM of the gray to black shales usually consists of only two components (Figures 4d-4f). First removed with a maximum unblocking temperature of 300 ø to sometimes 400øC is a steep downward magnetization which we identify as a recent overprint and refer to as the A component. A magnetization with moderate downward direction, analogous to the B component of the red sediments, is evidently not present in the magnetite-bearing gray shales. Instead, the remaining magnetization usually converges toward the origin by 560 ø to 575øC and has a shallow direction with a declination that roughly either parallels or is opposite to that of the A component; we regard this Cm component as the characteristic magnetization of the gray to black shales. A subset of the gray to black shales showed, at best, only a single linear trajectory that converged to the origin by about 300øC (Figure 4g). Magnetic susceptibility of samples from the Lockatong, Passaic, and Feltville Formations typically showed very large increases after heating to moderate to high temperatures, starting at about 550øC in the red and gray shales but by about 400øC in the darker gray to black shales (Figure 5). The growth of a highly magnetic phase may be related to alteration of clays or perhaps the oxidation of sulphides that are disseminated in much of the lacustrine sediments. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). The sedimentary sequence of the Budva Zone remained entirely pelagic from Trias to upper Cretaceous. It became detritic during the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) up to the Eocene when the flysch started to fill the preexisting basins. The Dalmate Zone (Kruja Zone in Albania) crops out in a narrow band all along the Adriatic coast and in all the eastern Adriatic islands (Figure 1). The Mesozoic sequence is entirely made of shelf limestones, very similar to the ones that outcrop in the Karst. For this reason the boundary between the Karst Zone and the Dalmate Zone is not clear in central and northern Dinarides. The calcareous sedimentation extends in the Dalmate Zone up to middle Eocene and is followed by middle- upper Eocene flysch. At the Eocene-Oligocene boundary the deformation reached the Dalmate Zone, which was divided in several tectonic units overthrusted onto the Adriatic foreland. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). The sedimentary sequence of the Budva Zone remained entirely pelagic from Trias to upper Cretaceous. It became detritic during the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) up to the Eocene when the flysch started to fill the preexisting basins. The Dalmate Zone (Kruja Zone in Albania) crops out in a narrow band all along the Adriatic coast and in all the eastern Adriatic islands (Figure 1). The Mesozoic sequence is entirely made of shelf limestones, very similar to the ones that outcrop in the Karst. For this reason the boundary between the Karst Zone and the Dalmate Zone is not clear in central and northern Dinarides. The calcareous sedimentation extends in the Dalmate Zone up to middle Eocene and is followed by middle- upper Eocene flysch. At the Eocene-Oligocene boundary the deformation reached the Dalmate Zone, which was divided in several tectonic units overthrusted onto the Adriatic foreland. This result contrasts with the very coherent post-Eocene 45 ø clockwise rotation previously observed in the external Albano-Hellenides from Peloponesus to the Tirana basin. These new results suggest that the Scutari-Pec line, located between the two orogens and considered as a Mesozoic transform fault on the basis of geological observations, is the place where the torsion between the Dinarides and the Albanides recently occurred. On a local scale, four sites (out of 10) from two ridges located in northern Albania, south of the Scutari-Pec line but with a Dinaric trend, show that these two structures have undergone a -30 ø post-Eocene clockwise rotation. This intermediate value of rotation between the north and the south suggests that the Scutari-Pec line is, in fact, a rather wide transversal zone in which the two ridges are located. It acted as a decoupling zone between the Dinarides and the Albano-Hellenides during the Cenozoic and probably until the Pleistocene time. Introduction It is now well-established that the geometry of the Mediterranean Alpine belt arises from the Upper Cretaceous- Cenozoic collision between the African and European plates [Tapponnier, 1977; Dercourt et al., 1986]. Kinematic reconstructions show that the collision is presently taking place at an average rate of roughly 1 cm/yr [Argus et al., 1989]. Yet in many domains, deformation rates greater by almost an order of magnitude have been documented [Le Pichon et al., 1993]. These high rates result from changing regional trends of the chains, formation of arcs, and recent back arc oceanic basins, which regionally modify the overall pattern of the collision. In this framework, paleomagnetic studies which allow the description of rotation about vertical axis have proven crucial to unravel the complex tectonic pattern and to allow palinspastic reconstruction. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). The sedimentary sequence of the Budva Zone remained entirely pelagic from Trias to upper Cretaceous. It became detritic during the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) up to the Eocene when the flysch started to fill the preexisting basins. The Dalmate Zone (Kruja Zone in Albania) crops out in a narrow band all along the Adriatic coast and in all the eastern Adriatic islands (Figure 1). The Mesozoic sequence is entirely made of shelf limestones, very similar to the ones that outcrop in the Karst. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. For all these reasons we decided to perform further paleomagnetic sampling. Sampling sites were selected in areas characterized by different orientation of the fold axes (from NW-SE in the Latium-Abruzzi platform to NE-SW in the southern Sabina area) and having different tectonic styles and deformation patterns. The sampled sequences range from upper Cretaceous to Messinian and represent the youngest sediments available for paleomagnetic studies in each structural domain. By sampling wide stratigraphic intervals in some particular structures (e.g., the Prenestini Mountains) we were able to obtain temporal control on the different rotations. Remaining samples were thermally demagnetized at 10 to 15 steps from room temperature up to the limit of reproducible results (320øC to 560øC). At each demagnetization step the bulk susceptibility was measured to monitor possible changes in magnetic mineralogy. Rock magnetic experiments, such as acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), alternating field demagnetization of the saturation IRM (SIRM) and thermal demagnetization analyses of three-component IRM [Lowrie, 1990] were performed on some representative samples. These analyses showed that the red samples from the Scaglia Formation are mainly characterized by low-coercivity minerals such as magnetite with a small amount of high- coercivity minerals such as hematite. The Guadagnolo Formation, the white samples of the Scaglia Formation, and some of the sites in Messinian clays are characterized by low- coercivity minerals with a blocking temperature of 580øC (Figure 3a). The tectonic setting of this region is characterized by NNW-SSE to N-S local structures resulting from the activity of transpressive mechanisms which have been recognized along the major N-S tectonic elements [Mattei and Miccadei, 1991; Ghisetti and Vezzani, 1991 ]. Low-Field Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) Results In the past few years AMS data yielded very important results concerning the strain history of rocks, in particular very weak or undeformed sedimentary sequences for which no other methods could be applied [Lowrie, 1989]. Although the AMS studies cannot substitute the petrofabric analyses in the strain studies, a strong correlation between the magnetic fabric detected by AMS analyses and the tectonic elements has been largely proved all around the world [Kligfield et al., 1981; Borradaile, 1988]. We measured AMS for sites sampled for paleomagnetic analyses. Data were analyzed using both the maximum density orientation and the tensorial statistics of Jelinek [1978]. The magnetic fabric is described by an ellipsoid in which Kmax, Kint, and Kmin represent the maximum, intermediate, and minimum axes. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. For all these reasons we decided to perform further paleomagnetic sampling. Rock magnetic experiments, such as acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), alternating field demagnetization of the saturation IRM (SIRM) and thermal demagnetization analyses of three-component IRM [Lowrie, 1990] were performed on some representative samples. Although the AMS studies cannot substitute the petrofabric analyses in the strain studies, a strong correlation between the magnetic fabric detected by AMS analyses and the tectonic elements has been largely proved all around the world [Kligfield et al., 1981; Borradaile, 1988]. Remaining samples were thermally demagnetized at 10 to 15 steps from room temperature up to the limit of reproducible results (320øC to 560øC). At each demagnetization step the bulk susceptibility was measured to monitor possible changes in magnetic mineralogy. Rock magnetic experiments, such as acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), alternating field demagnetization of the saturation IRM (SIRM) and thermal demagnetization analyses of three-component IRM [Lowrie, 1990] were performed on some representative samples. These analyses showed that the red samples from the Scaglia Formation are mainly characterized by low-coercivity minerals such as magnetite with a small amount of high- coercivity minerals such as hematite. Low-Field Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) Results In the past few years AMS data yielded very important results concerning the strain history of rocks, in particular very weak or undeformed sedimentary sequences for which no other methods could be applied [Lowrie, 1989]. Although the AMS studies cannot substitute the petrofabric analyses in the strain studies, a strong correlation between the magnetic fabric detected by AMS analyses and the tectonic elements has been largely proved all around the world [Kligfield et al., 1981; Borradaile, 1988]. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. For all these reasons we decided to perform further paleomagnetic sampling. Sampling sites were selected in areas characterized by different orientation of the fold axes (from NW-SE in the Latium-Abruzzi platform to NE-SW in the southern Sabina area) and having different tectonic styles and deformation patterns. The sampled sequences range from upper Cretaceous to Messinian and represent the youngest sediments available for paleomagnetic studies in each structural domain. By sampling wide stratigraphic intervals in some particular structures (e.g., the Prenestini Mountains) we were able to obtain temporal control on the different rotations. Low-Field Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) Results In the past few years AMS data yielded very important results concerning the strain history of rocks, in particular very weak or undeformed sedimentary sequences for which no other methods could be applied [Lowrie, 1989]. Although the AMS studies cannot substitute the petrofabric analyses in the strain studies, a strong correlation between the magnetic fabric detected by AMS analyses and the tectonic elements has been largely proved all around the world [Kligfield et al., 1981; Borradaile, 1988]. We measured AMS for sites sampled for paleomagnetic analyses. Data were analyzed using both the maximum density orientation and the tensorial statistics of Jelinek [1978]. The magnetic fabric is described by an ellipsoid in which Kmax, Kint, and Kmin represent the maximum, intermediate, and minimum axes. The anisotropy degree (P'), the foliation (F) and the lineation (L) parameters were also examined to determine the shape parameters of the susceptibility ellipsoid [Hrouda, 1982]. Magnetic fabric and paleomagnetic analyses on sedimentary sequences in several structural units in the Central Apennines ranging from upper Cretaceous pelagic carbonates to upper Miocene turbidites provide evidence for at least two distinct phases of rotation. The first counterclockwise (CCW) rotation is well recorded in Eocene-Oligocene sediments and does not affect the lower-middle Miocene sequences. The second phase is clearly recorded in lower-middle and upper Miocene sediments and shows both CCW and clockwise (CW) rotations in concordance with trends of the different thrust structures. We detected three domains characterized by different rotation patterns. The westernmost is the southern Sabina area, an arcuate thrust belt which underwent a CW rotation after the early Miocene. The second domain is the Latium-Abruzzi carbonate platform, where a CCW rotation occurred after the late Miocene. The third is the Marsica area that underwent a CW rotation after the late Miocene. The magnetic fabric analyses confirm the existence of these different structural provinces and show a strong correlation between the present- day strike of the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility magnetic lineation and the rotations recorded in Miocene sediments. We attribute present-day variations in orientation of the compressional structures in the Central Apennines to differential rotations about vertical axes due to strike-slip faults and out of sequence thrust activity, rather than to a change in the stress field orientation. We also suggest that this deformation mechanism could be common in other collisional chains around the world. Brief Summary of Paleomagnetic Research in Italy The paleomagnetic data collected in sedimentary sequences throughout the Italian peninsula show different patterns of rotation of the various geodynamic units. The Jurassic and Cretaceous sequences of the Apennines provide pieces of evidence for counterclockwise rotations of both the deformed Apenninic chain and the autochthonous Adriatic promontory with respect to the African VGP (see Lowrie [1986] and Channell [1992] for a review on this subject). Introduction Structural and stratigraphic data suggest that complex patterns of deformation are common in the Neogene collisional chains within the Mediterranean region. This complexity is mainly expressed by the coexistence of thrust, normal, and strike-slip faults arranged in different structural domains, as seen, for example, in the Aegean area and in the Betic Cordillera. Clockwise rotations of the Marsica and Maiella structures with respect to the Gargano and Umbria areas have been proposed [Jackson, 1990; Marton and D'Andrea, 1992], whereas large counterclockwise rotations have been measured in the Gran Sasso chain, explaining its E- W strike [Dela Pierre et al., 1992]. The number and the age of rocks sampled for these paleomagnetic studies, however, do not allow a complete reconstruction of the Neogene tectonic evolution and of the rotations pattern that affected the numerous structural units cropping out in the Central Apennines. To better understand the region's complex deformation, shown in Figure 1, we performed new structural and paleomagnetic analyses in Cretaceous to upper Miocene sedimentary sequences cropping out in some of the main structures. The present-day geometry of the Central Apennines has been explained with different models: (1) sequential deformation phases each characterized by a different orientation of the stress field [Castellarin et al., 1978; Salvini and Vittori, 1982]; (2) arcuate geometry related to out-of- sequence thrust sheets, following the eastward retreat of the subducting Adriatic lithosphere [Royden and Karner, 1984; Royden et al., 1987; Doglioni, 1991], separated by major N-S oriented right-lateral strike-slip faults [Patacca and Scandone, 1987; Patacca et al., 1990]. The complex tectonic evolution has also been related to the general counterclockwise rotation of the Italian peninsula indicated by paleomagnetic data collected in the past twenty years. We inves

The region is characterized by several thrust sheets oriented mainly NNW-SSE, although the presence of N-S to N30øE right-lateral strike-slip faults with associated back thrusts and minor strike-slip faults suggests that strike-slip faulting was also important in the tectonic evolution of this area [Corrado et al., 1990; Ghisetti and Vezzani, 1991; Mattei and Miccadei, 1991 ]. Abundant stratigraphic and structural data collected in the past few years have shown that the available paleomagnetic record is inadequate to reflect the tectonic complexity and the age of the deformation in this region. In particular, the present-day structure of the Apenninic chain has been described as the result of tectonic deformation that began after late Miocene times and continued very rapidly during Plio- Pleistocene times. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. rance Abstract. Magnetic fabric and paleomagnetic analyses on sedimentary sequences in several structural units in the Central Apennines ranging from upper Cretaceous pelagic carbonates to upper Miocene turbidites provide evidence for at least two distinct phases of rotation. The first counterclockwise (CCW) rotation is well recorded in Eocene-Oligocene sediments and does not affect the lower-middle Miocene sequences. The second phase is clearly recorded in lower-middle and upper Miocene sediments and shows both CCW and clockwise (CW) rotations in concordance with trends of the different thrust structures. We detected three domains characterized by different rotation patterns. The westernmost is the southern Sabina area, an arcuate thrust belt which underwent a CW rotation after the early Miocene. The second domain is the Latium-Abruzzi carbonate platform, where a CCW rotation occurred after the late Miocene. The third is the Marsica area that underwent a CW rotation after the late Miocene. The magnetic fabric analyses confirm the existence of these different structural provinces and show a strong correlation between the present- day strike of the anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility magnetic lineation and the rotations recorded in Miocene sediments. We attribute present-day variations in orientation of the compressional structures in the Central Apennines to differential rotations about vertical axes due to strike-slip faults and out of sequence thrust activity, rather than to a change in the stress field orientation. We also suggest that this deformation mechanism could be common in other collisional chains around the world. Brief Summary of Paleomagnetic Research in Italy The paleomagnetic data collected in sedimentary sequences throughout the Italian peninsula show different patterns of rotation of the various geodynamic units. The Jurassic and Cretaceous sequences of the Apennines provide pieces of evidence for counterclockwise rotations of both the deformed Apenninic chain and the autochthonous Adriatic promontory with respect to the African VGP (see Lowrie [1986] and Channell [1992] for a review on this subject). Counterclockwise rotations detected in lower Pleistocene rocks in the Southern Apennines [Sagnotti, 1992; Scheepers et al., 1993] and clockwise rotations detected in lower Pleistocene rocks in Southern Calabria and Sicily indicate the very young age of the bending of the Calabrian arc [Tauxe et al., 1983; Aifa et al., 1988; Scheepers et al., 1993; Scheepers and Langereis, 1993; Scheepers et al., 1994]. Introduction Structural and stratigraphic data suggest that complex patterns of deformation are common in the Neogene collisional chains within the Mediterranean region. This complexity is mainly expressed by the coexistence of thrust, normal, and strike-slip faults arranged in different structural domains, as seen, for example, in the Aegean area and in the Betic Cordillera. Paleomagnetic data from these regions show rotations of several structural units and suggest that rotations of large crustal blocks about the vertical axis accompanied the development of

Clockwise rotations of the Marsica and Maiella structures with respect to the Gargano and Umbria areas have been proposed [Jackson, 1990; Marton and D'Andrea, 1992], whereas large counterclockwise rotations have been measured in the Gran Sasso chain, explaining its E- W strike [Dela Pierre et al., 1992]. The number and the age of rocks sampled for these paleomagnetic studies, however, do not allow a complete reconstruction of the Neogene tectonic evolution and of the rotations pattern that affected the numerous structural units cropping out in the Central Apennines. To better understand the region's complex deformation, shown in Figure 1, we performed new structural and paleomagnetic analyses in Cretaceous to upper Miocene sedimentary sequences cropping out in some of the main structures. The present-day geometry of the Central Apennines has been explained with different models: (1) sequential deformation phases each characterized by a different orientation of the stress field [Castellarin et al., 1978; Salvini and Vittori, 1982]; (2) arcuate geometry related to out-of- sequence thrust sheets, following the eastward retreat of the subducting Adriatic lithosphere [Royden and Karner, 1984; Royden et al., 1987; Doglioni, 1991], separated by major N-S oriented right-lateral strike-slip faults [Patacca and Scandone, 1987; Patacca et al., 1990]. The complex tectonic evolution has also been related to the general counterclockwise rotation of the Italian peninsula indicated by paleomagnetic data collected in the past twenty years. We inves

asinal type [Colacicchi and Praturlon, 1965; Praturlon, 1968]. The region is characterized by several thrust sheets oriented mainly NNW-SSE, although the presence of N-S to N30øE right-lateral strike-slip faults with associated back thrusts and minor strike-slip faults suggests that strike-slip faulting was also important in the tectonic evolution of this area [Corrado et al., 1990; Ghisetti and Vezzani, 1991; Mattei and Miccadei, 1991 ]. Abundant stratigraphic and structural data collected in the past few years have shown that the available paleomagnetic record is inadequate to reflect the tectonic complexity and the age of the deformation in this region. In particular, the present-day structure of the Apenninic chain has been described as the result of tectonic deformation that began after late Miocene times and continued very rapidly during Plio- Pleistocene times. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. Gillen Abstract: The Rainbow Field is in reefal carbonates of the Middle Devonian Keg River Formation in the Western Can - ada Sedimentary Basin. Alternating field and thermal step demagnetization was done on specimens from unoriented core from a vertical, an inclined, and a horizontal well core in the dolomite reservoir. Although they had no viscous remanent magnetization component to use for orientation, most specimens had a well-defined characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) that resides in single to pseudosingle domain magnetite. By rotating the mean ChRM direction around its core axis, a small circle can be generated for each core and the small circles intersect in the true ChRM di - rection of D = 168°, I = –73.5 o (a 95 = 5.8°, k = 32.2). Its paleopole of 164°E, 83°N (A 95 = 10°) defines a Tertiary age with one sigma limits of Middle Eocene to Middle Miocene age. Petrographic examination defines four generations of dolomite. Matrix dolomite has 60–100 m m diameter crystals that were later recrystallized to 200–400 m m. If core is available from three or more wells with substan - tially different orientations, then it is possible to use the measured ChRM both to date its time of acquisition and to orient the cores. The “three-well ChRM” method of core ori - entation uses a triangulation technique similar to that used to determine the bedding or fabric dip direction from un - oriented well cores (see p. 161, Ramsay and Huber 1989; V ersteeg and Morris 1994). This is done by determining the mean inclination of the ChRM for each well relative to the well’s axis. Rotating the inclination about the axis generates a small circle on a stereonet, and the three small circles from the three wells will intersect in the only geographic orienta - tion for the ChRM that is permissible within statistical error. Each core can then be oriented by matching its measured ChRM to the calculated vector orientation. The field consists of several pools in strati - graphic traps formed by carbonate pinnacle-reef buildups of the Upper Keg River Member that are enclosed by evaporites and bituminous limestones of the overlying Muskeg Formation (Schmidt et al. 1985). Recently, however, it has been recog - nized that paleomagnetic methods can provide several types of valuable information for hydrocarbon exploration (Turner and Turner 1995). One of its uses is to orient drill core into its in situ geographic coordinates after it has been in storage for several years to determine, for example, the orientation of a reservoir’s fracture system. The orientation can be done paleomagnetically in two ways. The common method is to use the viscous remanent mag- netization (VRM). This is done by measuring the lower tem- perature or lower coercivity VRM component in the core and then aligning its direction to the present Earth’s dipole magnetic field (PEMF) direction using the well’s orientation as the rotational axis (V an der V oo and Watts 1978). A mod - ern VRM is usually preserved in petroliferous carbonate strata but it often requires very sensitive paleomagnetic in - strumentation to measure it. Most researchers accept the use of the PEMF direction for a reference (e.g., V an der V oo and Watts 1978; Kodama 1984), however Rolph et al. Most researchers accept the use of the PEMF direction for a reference (e.g., V an der V oo and Watts 1978; Kodama 1984), however Rolph et al. (1995) have recently suggested using the geographic or time- averaged Earth’s dipole magnetic field (GEMF). They argue that 730 000 years of spontaneous realignment since the last major polarity reversal will be preserved in the VRM. While this is true, the acquisition or decay of VRM is logarithmic with time, so that a short time period in the recent past may still represent a much larger fraction of the VRM signal. To date, we have found that the PEMF provides a better refer - ence (Lewchuk et al. 1998). Most cores also preserve a higher temperature or higher coercivity characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) component. Typically it has been ignored in VRM core- orientation studies because it is time consuming, often more difficult to isolate, and it has less direct utility. Nevertheless, if the core can be oriented by its VRM or by some other method, then the ChRM can be compared to the cratonic ap - parent polar wander path (APWP) to date its time of acquisi - tion (e.g., Perroud et al. 1995; Lewchuk et al. 1998). In this way, for example, unfossiliferous strata with a primary ChRM can be dated or, alternatively, a secondary diagenetic event such as dolomitization, which remagnetizes the strata with a secondary ChRM, can be dated. During this study, several planktic foraminifera were identi- fied (with the help of F.-J. Sierro personal communication, 1993). Only the genus Globigerinoides, which first appeared in the basal Miocene and is still living today, is recognized with certainty. Two specimens from about 10 m above the hardground could be either Globorotalia puncticulata or G. in- flata that are distributed from the early Pliocene to present. Specimens located about 40 m below the hardground were de- termined as either Globigerinoides extremus or G. congloba- tus, whose first appearance occurs during middle Tortonian. These age determinations are in fair agreement with those pre- sented by Chevalier [1968] and with the proposed rhodo- liths/corals transition age; the disappearance of the rhodoliths and its systematic replacement by corals in the SW Pacific are interpreted as the result of a climatic crisis during the late Miocene-Pliocene [Bourrouilh-Le Jan, 1979]. These geodynamic changes are constrained by magnetostratigraphically dating two sections from Mar6 Island, where mineral extractions coupled with rock-magnetic experiments suggest that the magnetic remanence is mostly carried by a mixture of single-domain to multidomain magnetite/ maghemite. Our objectives are to docu- ment the timing of the atoll construction and to discuss its evolution related to an active plate boundary. They are bounded to the east by the New Hebrides deep trench oriented 340øN, the site of the subduction (Figure l a). Mar6 is presently surrounded by living fringing reefs and has an atoll morphology with a peripheral rim and a central depression (Figure 2). The island consists of a volcanic base- ment overlain by two lithologically distinct carbonate se- quences partially dolomitized, which are uplifted to a maxi- mum of 138 m above sea level and tilted to the NE. Following the end of the volcanic activity, the basaltic substratum was subjected to marine erosion, and fringing reefs colonized its flanks, as shown by the presence of remobilized basalt blocks within the carbonate sediments [Koch, 1958]. In front of the reefs, an exclusive rhodolith sedimentation developed and progressively buried the volcano almost to the top, forming a vast platform. Rhodoliths are sub-spherical nodules, 5 to 10 cm in diameter, composed of red algae (Rhodophyte) and en- crusting foraminifera laminations [Bosellini and Ginsburg, 1971]. During this study, several planktic foraminifera were identi- fied (with the help of F.-J. Sierro personal communication, 1993). Only the genus Globigerinoides, which first appeared in the basal Miocene and is still living today, is recognized with certainty. Two specimens from about 10 m above the hardground could be either Globorotalia puncticulata or G. in- flata that are distributed from the early Pliocene to present. Specimens located about 40 m below the hardground were de- termined as either Globigerinoides extremus or G. congloba- tus, whose first appearance occurs during middle Tortonian. These age determinations are in fair agreement with those pre- sented by Chevalier [1968] and with the proposed rhodo- liths/corals transition age; the disappearance of the rhodoliths and its systematic replacement by corals in the SW Pacific are interpreted as the result of a climatic crisis during the late Miocene-Pliocene [Bourrouilh-Le Jan, 1979]. A warming of the climate during late Miocene-Pliocene would then have favored the de- velopment of corals. Based on the Mar6 sequences, we have no arguments either to infer or support a climatic crisis relation- ship. However, by dating precisely for the first time the rhodoliths/corals transition between 6.04 and 4.17 Ma, the present study confirms a major event, possibly of global scale, at the Miocene-Pliocene transition. Conclusion The present study reports the presence of a primary stable remanent magnetism carried mostly by single-domain to mul- tidomain magnetite/maghemite of late Miocene to Pliocene age, confirming that the widespread late Cenozoic shallow-wa- ter carbonates are amenable for paleomagnetic dating. Mar6 is presently surrounded by living fringing reefs and has an atoll morphology with a peripheral rim and a central depression (Figure 2). The island consists of a volcanic base- ment overlain by two lithologically distinct carbonate se- quences partially dolomitized, which are uplifted to a maxi- mum of 138 m above sea level and tilted to the NE. Following the end of the volcanic activity, the basaltic substratum was subjected to marine erosion, and fringing reefs colonized its flanks, as shown by the presence of remobilized basalt blocks within the carbonate sediments [Koch, 1958]. In front of the reefs, an exclusive rhodolith sedimentation developed and progressively buried the volcano almost to the top, forming a vast platform. The first component (A) removed (Figure 3a), usually by 300øC, has an in situ direction similar to that of the present-day field (I -- 59.3 ø, D - 14.5 ø) and recent axial-dipole field (I = 5 4.1 o, D = 0.0 ø) for southern California (Figure 7). This component could be either a recently acquired thermoviscous magnetization, one related to deep burial (several kilometers) followed by regional uplift in the late Tertiary [see Pullaiah et al., 1975], or a composite of both. The second component (B') removed (Figures 3b and 3c), usually between 100 ø and 500øC, is found only in samples from Goat Rock. The B' component (Figure 8) is similar to the overprint direction observed in pillow basalts and overlying Upper Jurassic sedimentary rocks of the Coast Range ophio- lite at Stanley Mountain [McWilliams and Howell, 1982; Hag- strum, 1992; Hagstrum and Murchey, 1995]. This component is interpreted as an overprint magnetization and its direction possibly indicates clockwise vertical-axis rotation (-50 ø ) of the Stanley Mountain and Goat Rock block similar to those doc- umented in the western Transverse Ranges [Hornafius et al., 1986], assuming that these rocks have not been significantly tilted since the Miocene. Samples from the chert sequence in Redrock Canyon mostly have southerly declination magnetizations (Figure 2) which may be due to random sampling where zones with northerly declination magnetizations were missed, possibly combined with fault repetition of section. The Redrock chert samples also have a significantly different characteristic magnetization than the underlying pillow basalts (D. Smith et al., personal communication, 1993). SUMMARY To evaluate suggestions from earlier work that a reversal of magnetization is present in the Rajmahal Traps of mid-Cretaceous (probable Aptian) age in north-eastern India, we have sampled a 140m thick section comprising a minimum of nine flow units at 25 sites in the north-western part of the outcrop. A coherent N+R+N magnetostratig- raphy is identified, with evidence for transitional behaviour at the top and bottom of the succession. The mean characteristic remanence direction of the reversed sites (D/I = 145.7"/63.5", ay5 = 6.0") is approximately antiparallel to that of the normal polarity sites (D/I = 300.2"/- 55.7", ay5 = 12.4"), and the group mean confirms a palaeomagnetic pole position near 125"E, 9"s (Ay5= 10.5") for the time of eruption of the traps. From 4oAr/39Ar evidence that the Rajmahal-Bengal Traps were emplaced over a short interval at ca. 117 Ma, we interpret the brief reversed episode identified near the base of the succession as a record of the ISEA event. The polarity evidence therefore supports the view that the Rajmahal Traps were fed by the Crozet Hotspot at the beginning of the Cretaceous Normal Superchron (- 119-83 Ma). Key words: magnetostratigraphy, palaeomagnetism, Rajmahal Traps. 1 INTRODUCTI

In addition, there have been a number of phases of lava-dome formation, and minor basaltic, andesitic and dacitic lavas are also found (Wilson et al. 1995). The identification and eruptive histories of the various volcanic centres are described in several volcanostratigraphic studies (Cole 1979; Wilson et al. 1984; Wilson, Houghton & Lloyd 1986; Nairn, Wood & Bailey 1994). The Rotorua, Okataina, Reporoa, Maroa and Taupo volcanic centres have all formed since 250 ka, and portions of the caldera margins are recognizable modern topographic features. The Whakamaru, Kapenga and Mangakino volcanic centres are older structures, largely obscured by younger faulting, volcanism and sedimentary fill, and have been ident- ified from geophysical and volcanological evidence. Fig. l(b) is a simplified geological map redrawn from Cole (1979), in which ignimbrites originating from the TVZ are distinguished from others and from the Mesozoic basement. Unit names, ages, latitude and longitude and NZ grid references (1 : 50000 series) of the sites are summarized in Appendix A, together with the palaeomagnetic results. Palaeomagnetic measurements were made at both Tokyo Institute of Technology and Victoria University of Wellington. In most cases, two pilot specimens from each site were demag- netized at each laboratory: one by stepwise alternating field (AF) and one by stepwise thermal demagnetization (i.e. at least four specimens from each site were demagnetized in detail). At most sites three to four more specimens were AF demag- netized to an appropriate peak field, usually between 10 and 25 mT, to remove secondary components of magnetization. However, at sites which showed intermediate palaeodirections or non-convergent natural remanent magnetization (NRM) directions, all specimens were carefully AF demagnetized in a progressive manner. Conclusions References The portion of the lztaccihuatl volcano above timberline and other volcanoes immediately to the north and to the south of the main mountain were found to have normal magnetic polarity. These data are consistent with, but not sufficient proof of, Mooser's hypothesis that the Knees, Breast, and Head originated during the Quaternary, a hypo- thesis which is contradicted by the improbable 13.3 my K-Ar age for the Knees as described above. A positive conglomerate test has been achieved on ten basalt clasts from a pyroclastic bre. ccia in the E'meishan basaltic sequence from Southwest China. Nine basalt samples collected from a nearby lava flow yield ChRM directions similar to the northeasterly and shallow up directions reported from elsewhere in the basalt province. This effectively refutes the suggestion that this group of directions represents a remagnetization of as late as J

ring paleomagnetic investigation on the Late Permian Emeishan Basalt from a type section in Southwest China that was followed by many later studies (Lin, 1984; Huang et al., 1986; Liu et al., 1987; Zhou et al., 1988; Zhao and Coe, 1989; Van der Voo et al., 1993). However, uncertainty still lingers as to whether the observed characteristic direction is primary or secondary. The lingering doubts of remagnetization mainly originate from differences of mean directions from different localities and lack of antipodality between the northeasterly and shallow up directions and the reversed southwesterly down directions. Although a positive fold test has been achieved for the northeasterly directions in some of the studies (McElhinny et al., 1981; Van der Voo et al., 1993), it only demonstrates at best that the acquisition of the magnetization predates the earliest Tertiary, which is the generally accepted age of folding that is much younger than the age of the rocks. A field test to better constrain the age of the ChRM has thus become very much needed. To this end, we recently conducted a conglomerate test on pyroclastic breccia from the basaltic sequence. Huang and N. D. 0pdyke Department of Goology, University of Florida, Gainesville Abstract. A positive conglomerate test has been achieved on ten basalt clasts from a pyroclastic bre. ccia in the E'meishan basaltic sequence from Southwest China. Nine basalt samples collected from a nearby lava flow yield ChRM directions similar to the northeasterly and shallow up directions reported from elsewhere in the basalt province. This effectively refutes the suggestion that this group of directions represents a remagnetization of as late as Jurassic or Triassic age. The difference between different sets of results from the Emeishan Basalt and the non-antipodality between the northeasterly directions and the reversed southwesterly down directions are likely to be due to a combination of minor structural rotations about vertical axes between the sampled localities, inaccuracy in determination of bedding attitude in massive basaltic rocks, and insufficient paleomagnetic sampling. The difference between different sets of results from the Emeishan Basalt and the non-antipodality between the northeasterly directions and the reversed southwesterly down directions are likely to be due to a combination of minor structural rotations about vertical axes between the sampled localities, inaccuracy in determination of bedding attitude in massive basaltic rocks, and insufficient paleomagnetic sampling. Introduction McElhinny and his collaborators (1981) conducted a pioneering paleomagnetic investigation on the Late Permian Emeishan Basalt from a type section in Southwest China that was followed by many later studies (Lin, 1984; Huang et al., 1986; Liu et al., 1987; Zhou et al., 1988; Zhao and Coe, 1989; Van der Voo et al., 1993). However, uncertainty still lingers as to whether the observed characteristic direction is primary or secondary. The lingering doubts of remagnetization mainly originate from differences of mean directions from different localities and lack of antipodality between the northeasterly and shallow up directions and the reversed southwesterly down directions. Although a positive fold test has been achieved for the northeasterly directions in some

ntipodality between the northeasterly and shallow up directions and the reversed southwesterly down directions. Although a positive fold test has been achieved for the northeasterly directions in some of the studies (McElhinny et al., 1981; Van der Voo et al., 1993), it only demonstrates at best that the acquisition of the magnetization predates the earliest Tertiary, which is the generally accepted age of folding that is much younger than the age of the rocks. A field test to better constrain the age of the ChRM has thus become very much needed. To this end, we recently conducted a conglomerate test on pyroclastic breccia from the basaltic sequence. The samples studied include alluvial sandstones and mudstones as well as shallow lacustrine and paludine, micritic and microsparitic limestones. Two-hundred-and-fifty specimens were stepwise thermally or magnetically demagnetized following standard procedures. Magnetic imprints of the distinct lithologies present sharp contrasts, especially for the stability of the secondary components. The VGP data show 18 reversal events, defining a sequence of 16 polarity intervals. Lateral and vertical continuity of the sequences studied has enabled a correspondence between the local paleomastological biozones and the magnetostratigraphic succession to be established. The high-resolution chronology of this magnetostratigraphic succession provides valuable information that allows the non-marine European biochronological scales to be correlated to the global polarity time scale (GPTS). best preserved diabase dyke, as determined by petrographic and bulk magnetization properties, carries both the A R magnetization and the A N magnetization as a secondary component in some samples. The most altered diabase dyke is almost completely overprinted by A N. The overprinting has taken place as a result of hydrothermal alteration and formation of new magnetite during the emplacement of quartz porphyry dykes and rapakivi granite. The quartz porphyries and diabases carry mixed SD and MD magnetic grain sizes, the large MD grains being responsible for a relatively large Present Earth's Field (PEF) magnetization. In addition, a high coercivity magnetization B (D = 23.9 °, I = 52.2 °, k = 215.8, a95 = 6.3 °, n = 4 dykes), presumably a chemical overprint, has been isolated in the quartz porphyries. The B magnetization is interpreted to be either an intermediate direction between A N and PEF with no geological significance, or to represent a separate reactivation of the crust at about 1.32 Ga ago. I. Introduction Subjotnian time (1600-1300 Ma) in Fenno- scandia is characterized by anorogenic magma- tism comprising large volumes of rapakivi gran- ites and associated dyke rocks. Palaeomagneti- cally the Subjotnian is defined by a self-closing loop of the Apparent Polar Wan

ess than 5 ° . Thirty-one samples were taken from five diabase dykes (Fig. 2) and 64 from nine quartz porphyry dykes. In order to carry out baked contact tests, 22 samples were taken from the host migmatites and gran- ites. Unfortunately, full baked contact tests of either diabase or quartz porphyry dykes were not successful owing to too weak intensities and un- stable remanences of the host rocks. In the laboratory, two to five standard 2.5 × 2.2 cm specimens were cut from each sample. All samples were subjected to stepwise alternating field (AF) demagnetization up to 100 mT in steps of 5 or 10 mT using Schonstedt instruments. Thermal demagnetizations were done by Schonst- edt furnace in 50 ° or 100°C intervals below 500°C and in 10 ° or 20°C intervals up to 680°C. Suscep- tibilities were measured after each thermal de- magnetization step in order to detect mineralogi- cal changes related to heating. AF demagnetiza- tion proved to be a better method in isolating different components both in diabases and quartz porphyries. Remanence measurements were done using self-made or JR4 spinner magnetometers. Principal component analysis (Kirschvink, 1980) was used to calculate the remanence com- ponents. Maximum angular deviation (MAD) val- ues of individual linear segments, defined by at least three demagnetization points, were usually 6 ° and in a few cases 15 °. Petrophysical properties (NRM intensity, low field susceptibility and density) were measured on each specimen. Saturation isothermal remanent magnetization (SIRM) was induced in a field of 1.4 T for seven samples. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility (AMS) was measured from seven diabase samples and from nine quartz porphyry samples using the KLY-2 kappabridge (manufac- tured by Geofysika Brno). Quartz porphyries Quartz porphyries are weakly magnetized, but stable directions were obtained from dykes SA, FA, PN, PV and PS (Fig. 2). In dykes PO, PR, SE and TV detailed AF and thermal demagnetiza- tion studies either did not reveal any consistent direction of the NRM at all or only yielded direc- tions corresponding to the Present Earth's Field (PEF) in the sample location. Thus, data from those dykes were rejected. In the quartz por- phyries carrying stable magnetizations, three components were typically identified; a low- coercivity PEF, an intermediate-coercivity A N component and a high-coercivity B component (Fig. 3, Table 1). The soft com- ponent is removed in low peak fields of the order of 5-10 mT and it is close to the PEF direction. e dyke sets of southern Finland and cut sharply the Svecofennian bedrock. The width of the dyke swarm is about 80 km and it can be followed over 20 km distance. Dykes are mostly vertical or subvertical. The strike of most quartz porphyry dykes is northwest-southeast, while the direction of the diabases trends more west-east. The width of the quartz porphyry dykes ranges from some centimetres to 25 m, the typical width is about 3-5 m. The dykes are fine grained with aphanitic contacts (T6rnroos, 1984). The main constituents are K-feldspar, quartz and plagio- clase and the accessories are biotite, hornblende, apatite, fluorite and magnetite-ilmenite. Primary biotite and amphibole indicate that the magma was hydrous (T6rnroos, 1984). The K-feldspar phenocrysts can be up to 2 cm long, while the quartz and plagioclase phenocrysts are smaller. In some quartz porphyry dykes, there are plagio- clase and magnetite-ilmenite phenocrysts in an orb-like spherulitic groundmass (T6rnroos, 1984). The heat required for thermal remagnetization was produced during extension and rifting of New Zealand and the Campbell Plateau from Marie Byrd Land, the event which also supplied heat for anatexis in the Fosdick Complex [Smith, 1992]. Cretaceous remagnetization is also suspected in northern Victoria Land from several paleomagnetic studies on a variety of rocks of differing ages [Delisle and Fromm, 1984, 1989; Schmierer and Burmester, 1986; Lanza and Zanella, 1993]. Evidence for remagnetization includes uniform normal polarity and anomalous high-latitude pole positions. Partial thermal viscous remanence magnetization experiments (vPTRM) were done on samples by Schmierer and Burmester [1986], who concluded that viscous thermal remagnetization was indeed possible. Lanza and Zanella [1993] came to the opposite conclusion in their experiments, but we note that if a 10 million year long period for remagnetization is assumed, their experiments also could confirm the remagnetization hypothesis. Magnetic overprinting attributed to vPTRM during Cretaceous rifting has also been observed in rocks from southeast Australia [Schmidt and Embleton, 1981]. In practice, small-circle distributions would be difficult to distinguish from great-circle distributions caused by proces- ses other than simple tilting, by differential tilting, partial overprinting, or magnetic anisotropy, for example, and these possibilities need to be investigated. On these bases, we argue that tilting is the most likely cause of the elongate dis- tribution. York Abstract: The Porteau Pluton is a variably foliated quartz diorite to granodiorite intrusion in the southern Coast Belt of the Canadian Cordillera (49.6"N, 123.2"W). 40Ar/39Ar ages are 95 f 5 Ma from biotite and 101.5 + 0.7 Ma from hornblende, which, together with an earlier U-Pb zircon age of 100 f 2 Ma, indicate that the body was emplaced, uplifted, and cooled rapidly in mid-Cretaceous time. The rocks contain high coercive force (hard) remanent magnetizations with unblocking temperatures between 500 and 600°C, close to those of Ar in hornblende, indicating that remanence was acquired at or close to the hornblende plateau age. The hard remanence directions have an elongate distribution, in agreement with the predictions of M.E. Beck regarding magnetization acquired during tilting, uplift, and cooling of plutons. No part of the distribution agrees with the direction expected from observations from rocks of mid-Cretaceous age from cratonic North America. The elongate distribution defines the axis of tilt (347" east of north) but not its direction; tilt could have been down toward the east or down toward the west. The former yields an inclination that is 29.0 f 4.9" shallower than expected from cratonic o

If a pluton is tilted at the same time as it is being uplifted and cooled, different parts of it would acquire a thermoremanent magnetization (TRM) at different stages during tilting. As a consequence, the directions of remanent magnetization would be distributed along a small circle centred on the horizontal axis of rotation (Beck 1991). In practice, small-circle distributions would be difficult to distinguish from great-circle distributions caused by proces- ses other than simple tilting, by differential tilting, partial overprinting, or magnetic anisotropy, for example, and these possibilities need to be investigated. We report paleomagnetic results from layered igneous rocks that imply substantial post mid-Cretaceous poleward mo- tion of the Insular superterrane (western Canadian Cordillera and southeast Alaska) relative to North America. The samples stud- ied are from the stratiform zoned ultramafic body at Duke Island, which intruded rocks of the Alexander terrane at the south end of the southeastern Alaska archipelago at about 110 Ma. Thermal and alternating field demagnetization experiments show that the characteristic remanence of the ultramafic rocks has high coer- civity and a narrow unblocking temperature range just below the Curie temperature of magnetite. This remanence is likely carried by low-Ti titanomagnetite exsolved within clinopyroxene and perhaps other silicate hosts. The Duke Island intrusion exhibits a well-developed gravitational layering that was deformed during initial cooling (but below 540øC) into folds that plunge moder- ately to the west-southwest. The characteristic remanence clearly predates this early folding and is therefore primary; the Fisher parameter describing the concentration of the overall mean rema- nence direction improves from 3 to 32 when the site-mean direc- tions are corrected by restoring the la

Ten samples were collected from each of two sites (HCS-1 and HCS-2) near the south end of Hall Cove, from three sites northwest of Hall Cove (HCN-1, HCN-2, and HCN-3), and from three sites at Judd Harbor (JH-1, JH-2, and JH-3). Analysis of the remanence was performed with a three-component cryogenic magnetometer, tumbling alternating field (AF) demagnetization apparatus, and a shielded oven that allowed heating of samples in air in a field of less than 2 nT. Stepwise AF demagnetization experiments were performed on nearly all samples. The number of demagnetization steps varied from sample to sample depending on the results of detailed pilot work on several samples from each site, with 7 to 10 steps up to 0.1 T being typical. Joseph/Precambrian Research 76 (1996) 31-46 We have collected 251 samples from 38 sites in four major dyke swarms in the high-grade metamorphic region and have systematically determined stable palaeomagnetic vectors. We have also obtained K-Ar and/or Rb-Sr isotopic ages corresponding to each swarm vector. Only one site proved to be a Cretaceous dyke. Our results provide a substantial Precambrian palaeomagnetic record for southern India enabling the drawing of an apparent polar wander curve for India for the Proterozoic. 2. Geology of the dyke swarms Numerous dyke intrusions occur within the high- grade crystalline basement of southern India (Fig. 1). Of these, the Agali-Anaikatti dykes (Fig. 2a) consti- tute an ENE-WSW swarm occurring along the Bhavani shear zone/lineament bordering the southern margin of the Nilgiri Massif (Fig. 1 ). The swarm is 20-25 km wide and extends from a few kilometres west of Agali to more than ~ 50 km towards the east in a general ENE-WSW direction. Some of the dykes show faint schistosity and subhorizontal lineations that correspond to shearing or a final phase of open folding wi

Conclusions The Precambrian rocks of northern Karelia, Russia have a complicated magnetization history. Their rem- anence is multicomponent and was caused by intense mafic-ultramafic magmatism at 2.47-2.35 Ga and by the later Svecofennian activity at 1.90-l.70 Ga of the Karelian craton. During Svecofennian times the rocks acquired overprints twice: in the early and in the late stage of the Svecofennian orogeny. The palaeomag- netic information combined with the known Protero- zoic endogenic activity allows us to conclude that the strength of these processes decreased from the early stages onwards. Another conclusion is that some stages of the endogenic activity were accompanied by altera- tions of the ferromagnetic minerals (e.g. high- and low- temperature oxidation). Conclusions The Precambrian rocks of northern Karelia, Russia have a complicated magnetization history. Their rem- anence is multicomponent and was caused by intense mafic-ultramafic magmatism at 2.47-2.35 Ga and by the later Svecofennian activity at 1.90-l.70 Ga of the Karelian craton. During Svecofennian times the rocks acquired overprints twice: in the early and in the late stage of the Svecofennian orogeny. The palaeomag- netic information combined with the known Protero- zoic endogenic activity allows us to conclude that the strength of these processes decreased from the early stages onwards. Another conclusion is that some stages of the endogenic activity were accompanied by altera- tions of the ferromagnetic minerals (e.g. high- and low- temperature oxidation). Later, at the early stage of formation of a volcanic-plutonic association, including layered intrusions and metavolcanites, gabbro-norite dykes were emplaced. Poles: A, B, D after Mertanen et al. (1989), northern Finland; A~, B~, C~ this work, northern Karelia; Cz, C3 after Krasnova and Gooskova (1990), southeastern Karelia (Burakovsky complex). 6. Conclusions The Precambrian rocks of northern Karelia, Russia have a complicated magnetization history. Their rem- anence is multicomponent and was caused by intense mafic-ultramafic magmatism at 2.47-2.35 Ga and by the later Svecofennian activity at 1.90-l.70 Ga of the Karelian craton. During Svecofennian times the rocks acquired overprints twice: in the early and in the late stage of the Svecofennian orogeny. The palaeomag- netic information combined with the known Protero- zoic endogenic activity allows us to conclude that the strength of these processes decreased from the early stages onwards. Another conclusion is that some stages of the endogenic activity were accompanied by altera- tions of the ferromagnetic minerals (e.g. high- and low- temperature oxidation). General geology The study area is located between the lakes Piaozero and Tikshozero. It is bordered by the Belomorian prov- ince (Fig. 1). The bedrock is composed of Archaean granites, granodiorites and migmatites. Basement rocks have undergone metamorphic and structural reworking more than once. There is a gradual transition between all the rock types. A comprehensive description of the geology is given by Shemiakin and Shoorkin (1974), Sidorenko (1974), Lavrov (1979), Ein (1982, 1984) and Stepanov (1984). Despite questions regarding the interpretation of K-Ar age determinations, the remark- able consistency of these ages and the bracketing of the age of the Gagwe lavas by other radiometric studies (De Paepe et al., 1991) leads to the conclusion that extrusion age of these lavas at 810 + 25 Ma is reliable. De Paepe et al. ( 1991 ) suggested that the most of the Bukoban Supergroup was deposited in a local basin during the interval 950-800 Ma. The tectonic setting of the Gagwe lavas is not clear. Chemical discrimina- tion diagrams are compatible with a convergent plate setting for the Gagwe and Kabuye lavas (De Paepe et al., 1991 ) but the authors noted that the data are scat- tered and offered as their preferred interpretation that the lavas erupted as continental flood basalts. The entire Bukoban Supergroup is only mildly deformed except near areas that were reactivated during Cenozoic exten- sion (De Paepe et al., 1991; Tack et al., 1992). The Gagwe lavas and the correlative Bukoban Intru- sives of Tanzania were the subject of a previous paleo- magnetic analysis (Piper, 1972) that yielded 228 J.G. Dodoma, Tanzania Received 16 August 1994; revised version accepted 27 February 1995 Abstract The 810 Ma Gagwe-Kabuye lavas and the 743 Ma Mbozi gabbro-syenite complex of the Congo Craton in East Africa were sampled for paleomagnetic study in an effort to test a variety of tectonic models proposed for Neoproterozoic times. The paleomagnetic pole obtained from the Gagwe-Kabuye lavas falls at 25°S, 273°E (81) = 7 °, 6m = 12 °) and compares favorably to a previously published paleomagnetic pole obtained from these rocks. The Mbozi complex pole yields a paleomagnetic pole at 46°N, 325°E ( 8p = 5 °, 8m = 9 °) and differs significantly from a previously determined pole for the Mbozi complex. A comparison of these paleomagnetic poles to Laurentian poles of the same age suggests that the Congo Craton may not have constituted part of the Rodinia superconti

le at 46°N, 325°E ( 8p = 5 °, 8m = 9 °) and differs significantly from a previously determined pole for the Mbozi complex. A comparison of these paleomagnetic poles to Laurentian poles of the same age suggests that the Congo Craton may not have constituted part of the Rodinia supercontinent in the configuration proposed by Dalziel (1992). An analysis of reliable paleomagnetic poles from the Gondwana blocks for the interval from 810 to 510 Ma reveals a coherent swathe of poles from 550 to 510 Ma and a scatter of pre-600 Ma poles. Our interpretation of the available paleomagnetic and tectonic data for this interval is consistent with the formation of Gondwana by two distinct orogenic events. This assembly resulted in the East Africa Orogen between 800 and 650 Ma and a younger Kuunga Orogen at 550 Ma outboard of the East Africa Orogen with possible sutures located in Sri Lanka, southern India and Enderby Land (East Antarctic Craton). 1. Introduction The Meso-Neoproterozoic interval from 1100 to 550 Ma is receiving an ever increasing amount of attention following the seminal papers of Moores (1991), Dal- ziel ( 1991 ) and Hoffman ( 1991 ). These three papers outline the Meso-Neoproterozoic (1100-750 Ma) links between Australia, Antarctica and the western margin of Laurentia (c

coherent unit from at least 1300 Ma until its breakup in the Mesozoic, but the concept of a coherent East Gondwana is questioned by Kr6ner (1993) and Meert and Van der Voo (1994). They propose that the East Gondwana continent is assembled through polyphase accretion of cratonic blocks between 800 and 550 Ma. Just as Rodinia assembled around Laurentia, the assembly of Gondwana can be viewed as Congo-centric and therefore knowledge of the position of the Congo Craton during this interval is critical in order to resolve the history of the amalga- mation of Gondwana and, by proxy, the breakup of Rodinia. With these issues in mind we sampled the Mbozi syenite complex in southern Tanzania (743 _+ 30 Ma) and the Gagwe lavas of western Tanzania and eastern Burundi (810 _+ 25 Ma) in an effort to constrain the position of the Congo Craton during this interval of supercontinental dispersal and assembly. 2. Dodoma, Tanzania Received 16 August 1994; revised version accepted 27 February 1995 Abstract The 810 Ma Gagwe-Kabuye lavas and the 743 Ma Mbozi gabbro-syenite complex of the Congo Craton in East Africa were sampled for paleomagnetic study in an effort to test a variety of tectonic models proposed for Neoproterozoic times. The paleomagnetic pole obtained from the Gagwe-Kabuye lavas falls at 25°S, 273°E (81) = 7 °, 6m = 12 °) and compares favorably to a previously published paleomagnetic pole obtained from these rocks. The Mbozi complex pole yields a paleomagnetic pole at 46°N, 325°E ( 8p = 5 °, 8m = 9 °) and differs significantly from a previously determined pole for the Mbozi complex. A comparison of these paleomagnetic poles to Laurentian poles of the same age suggests that the Congo Craton may not have constituted part of the Rodinia superconti

le at 46°N, 325°E ( 8p = 5 °, 8m = 9 °) and differs significantly from a previously determined pole for the Mbozi complex. A comparison of these paleomagnetic poles to Laurentian poles of the same age suggests that the Congo Craton may not have constituted part of the Rodinia supercontinent in the configuration proposed by Dalziel (1992). An analysis of reliable paleomagnetic poles from the Gondwana blocks for the interval from 810 to 510 Ma reveals a coherent swathe of poles from 550 to 510 Ma and a scatter of pre-600 Ma poles. Our interpretation of the available paleomagnetic and tectonic data for this interval is consistent with the formation of Gondwana by two distinct orogenic events. This assembly resulted in the East Africa Orogen between 800 and 650 Ma and a younger Kuunga Orogen at 550 Ma outboard of the East Africa Orogen with possible sutures located in Sri Lanka, southern India and Enderby Land (East Antarctic Craton). 1. Introduction The Meso-Neoproterozoic interval from 1100 to 550 Ma is receiving an ever increasing amount of attention following the seminal papers of Moores (1991), Dal- ziel ( 1991 ) and Hoffman ( 1991 ). They propose that the East Gondwana continent is assembled through polyphase accretion of cratonic blocks between 800 and 550 Ma. Just as Rodinia assembled around Laurentia, the assembly of Gondwana can be viewed as Congo-centric and therefore knowledge of the position of the Congo Craton during this interval is critical in order to resolve the history of the amalga- mation of Gondwana and, by proxy, the breakup of Rodinia. SMITH Department of Geology University of Auckland Private Bag 92 019 Auckland, New Zealand Abstract The South Auckland volcanic field is one of the Pliocene-Quaternary intraplate basaltic fields in northern North Island. It consists of at least 97 monogenetic volcanic centres covering an area of c. 300 km2, 38 km south of Auckland. Fifty-nine of the volcanic centres are characterised by mainly magmatic or effusive activity that constructed scoria cones and lava flows, while 38 are mainly phreatomagmatic or explosive that produced tuff rings and maars. Rock types consist of basanites, hawaiites, nepheline hawaiites, transitional basalts, and oZ-tholeiitic basalts, with relatively minor amounts of nephelinites, alkali basalts, Q- tholeiitic basalts, and nepheline mugearites. Forty-three new K-Ar ages are presented, which range from 0.51 to 1.59 Ma, and show two peaks of activity at 0.6 and 1.3 Ma. Paleomagnetic determinations at 26 selected sites agree well with the paleomagnetic reversal time scale and support the K-Ar age data. Age data from each of the volcanic fields of Okete, Ngatutura, South Auckland, and Auckland, which constitute the Auckland intraplate basaltic province, show tha

those of Northland where volcanic activity occurred over a long duration from 9.7 Ma ago (Smith et al. 1993) and extended up to 1800-1300 yr ago (Kear & Hay 1961). Twelve radiometric ages have been determined for the South Auckland volcanic field by Stipp (1968) and Robertson (1976), and the purpose of this paper is to present 43 new K-Ar ages, 26 paleomagnetic determinations, and to discuss some implications of these ages in terms of age patterns within the field. We also examine some preliminary geochemical data, in particular whether there are any relationships between age and composition of the volcanic rocks, and briefly describe their petrography. SOUTH AUCKLAND VOLCANIC FIELD The South Auckland volcanic field covers volcanic centres located west of Papakura and Drury in the north, Hunua Falls in the northeast, Pukekawa in the south, and extending to Waiuku in the west (Fig. 2).
